planting.note: Direct sow only, cilantro resents transplanting; sow in early spring or, in mild-winter climates, in fall for a longer cool-season harvest window.

directions: Sow seed directly into well-drained soil a quarter inch deep and thin to a few inches apart, since cilantro's taproot makes it a poor candidate for transplanting. Confetti is a fine-cut ornamental-leaf selection producing lacy, thread-like foliage instead of the broad lower leaves of standard cilantro, while keeping the same citrusy coriander flavor. Its dissected leaves make it a favorite for garnishing and for gardeners who want a distinct texture from a typical cilantro planting. Succession sow every few weeks in cool weather since, like all cilantro, it bolts quickly once temperatures climb into the 80s.

common_name: Jim Dandy Winterberry Holly (Early Male Pollinator Winterberry)

planting.note: Plant as a pollinator alongside compact early-blooming female cultivars such as Red Sprite; one Jim Dandy can pollinate several nearby females if bloom times overlap.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade, matching this male selection's early bloom time to an early-flowering female cultivar to ensure the berry set gardeners actually grow winterberry for. Jim Dandy itself produces no berries since winterberry is dioecious, but it is a compact, floriferous pollen source that stays proportionate to dwarf female cultivars rather than overwhelming them the way a full-size male can. Its small white spring flowers are inconspicuous but essential to fruiting nearby females. Prune only lightly and only after flowering, since flower buds form on the previous year's wood.
sources: University of Connecticut Home & Garden Education Center

common_name: Olympic Fire Mountain Laurel (Red-Budded Mountain Laurel)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; avoid soggy sites and heavy afternoon sun, which stresses mountain laurel in hot climates.

directions: Site in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled or part shade, mulching with pine bark or pine straw to hold moisture and acidity. Olympic Fire is a mountain laurel selection prized for exceptionally deep, wine-red buds that open to lighter pink flowers, giving a stronger two-tone contrast than the species' typical pink-and-white banding. It shares the species' gnarled, sculptural habit and evergreen foliage, making it a strong specimen or woodland-border shrub. Like all mountain laurel, every part of the plant is toxic if ingested.

common_name: Mountain Fire Japanese Pieris (Red New-Growth Andromeda)

planting.note: Plant container stock in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in part shade alongside azaleas and rhododendrons, which share the same cultural needs.

directions: Grow in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic soil in part shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and drying winter wind. Mountain Fire is grown chiefly for its brilliant fire-engine-red new growth in spring, considered among the most vivid of any Pieris cultivar, which matures to bronze and then glossy dark green as the season progresses. Cascading chains of small white urn-shaped flowers open in late winter to early spring before the new flush, giving two distinct ornamental moments. It is slow-growing and low-maintenance once established, needing little pruning beyond removing spent flower clusters.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, giving this fern generous room since it dwarfs typical painted and lady ferns.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Godzilla is a robust hybrid lady fern, similar in parentage to other silver-frosted Athyrium hybrids but selected and named for its outsized stature, forming a much larger clump with broader, more upright fronds than typical Athyrium cultivars. It carries a silvery overlay on the fronds inherited from its Japanese painted fern parentage while showing far greater vigor and heat tolerance than straight painted fern. Use it as a bold textural anchor in a shade border where a standard-size Athyrium would be lost, pairing it with hostas and heucheras for scale contrast.

planting.note: Plant in consistently moist to boggy, acidic, humus-rich soil in part shade to full sun near the water's edge; this cultivar tolerates more sun than most ferns if soil stays wet.

directions: Grow in consistently wet to moist, acidic, humus-rich soil at a pond or stream edge or in a rain garden, since royal fern tolerates standing water far better than most ferns. Purpurascens is distinguished from the species by fiddleheads and young fronds that emerge a deep reddish-purple before maturing toward green, giving strong spring color along with the species' coarse, almost shrub-like frond structure that reads more like a flowering perennial than a typical fern. Fertile fronds bear rust-colored spore clusters at their tips in summer, adding further textural interest. Divide congested clumps in early spring if needed, but otherwise this long-lived fern requires minimal care once sited correctly.
